title: MCAT (Medical College Admission Test)
description: Four-section, 7h 30min medical-school admissions exam. Three science sections (Bio/Biochem, Chem/Phys, Psych/Soc) plus CARS (Critical Analysis & Reasoning). Each section scored 118-132; total 472-528 (mean ~500).

sections.title: Chemical and Physical Foundations of Biological Systems

questions.promptMd: Which of the following best describes a covalent bond?

options.label: A
options.text: Transfer of electrons from metal to nonmetal.

options.label: B
options.text: Sharing of valence electrons between atoms.

options.label: D
options.text: Delocalized electron sea between metal atoms.

questions.explanationMd: Covalent bonds are defined by electron sharing. Choice A is ionic; C is also ionic; D describes metallic bonding.

questions.promptMd: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanationMd: F = ma, so the unit is kg·m/s² = newton (N). Joule is energy, pascal pressure, watt power.

questions.promptMd: A solution with pH 4 is how many times more acidic than pH 6?
questions.explanationMd: Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H+]. ΔpH = 2 → 10² = 100× more acidic.

questions.promptMd: Which functional group is present in an amide?
questions.explanationMd: An amide is R-C(=O)-N. B is a carboxylic acid, C is an ester, D is an alcohol.

questions.promptMd: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates from rest at 4 m/s². The net force on it is:
Which of the following is a common reducing agent in biological systems?
questions.explanationMd: NADH carries electrons (reduced form) and donates them to other molecules. NAD+ and FAD are oxidized; O₂ is the terminal oxidizer.

questions.promptMd: Which physical principle explains why blood pressure decreases as blood flows through capillaries (compared with arteries)?

options.label: A
options.text: Bernoulli's principle: faster flow → lower pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Continuity equation: total cross-sectional area increases → velocity drops → pressure drops.

questions.explanationMd: The collective cross-sectional area of all capillaries is far larger than the aorta's, so by continuity (A·v = constant for incompressible flow) velocity drops; combined with high resistance, pressure drops markedly.

questions.promptMd: A monoprotic weak acid HA has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of a 0.10 M solution?
Which mechanism is responsible for converting kinetic energy of moving fluid into pressure as the fluid slows down (e.g., in an aneurysm where vessel diameter increases)?
questions.explanationMd: Bernoulli's equation: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. As v drops, P rises — exactly what makes aneurysm pressures dangerous.

questions.promptMd: An SN2 reaction occurs most readily with:

options.label: D
options.text: Secondary alkyl halides + weak bases in protic solvent.

questions.explanationMd: SN2 needs unhindered backside attack — primary substrates — and a strong nucleophile to displace the leaving group concertedly.

questions.promptMd: A photon of frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz has energy approximately:
The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation predicts the pH of a buffer where pKa = 4.76 and [A⁻]/[HA] = 10. The pH is:
Which statement about enzyme kinetics is most accurate?

options.label: B
options.text: Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax.

options.label: C
options.text: Competitive inhibitors decrease Vmax but leave Km unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Noncompetitive inhibitors decrease Km but leave Vmax unchanged.

questions.explanationMd: Km = [S] at v = Vmax/2; this is its operational definition. Vmax depends on [enzyme], not [substrate]. Competitive inhibitors raise Km but leave Vmax. Noncompetitive lowers Vmax leaving Km unchanged.

questions.promptMd: An ideal gas undergoes isothermal expansion from 1 L to 2 L at 300 K. The work done by 1 mole of gas is approximately:
questions.explanationMd: W_by_gas = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 1 × 8.314 × 300 × ln(2) ≈ 1730 J. Positive sign means gas does work on surroundings.

questions.promptMd: In an aldol condensation, the rate-determining step typically involves:

options.label: C
options.text: Dehydration to give the α,β-unsaturated product.

questions.explanationMd: Enolate formation (deprotonation of α-carbon) is typically slow and rate-limiting; the subsequent addition is fast.

questions.promptMd: Light passes from air (n = 1.0) into glass (n = 1.5) at 30° from normal. The angle of refraction is:
questions.explanationMd: Snell's law: 1·sin(30°) = 1.5·sin(θ₂); sin(θ₂) = 0.333, θ₂ ≈ 19.5°.

questions.promptMd: Glycolysis converts one glucose molecule into:
questions.explanationMd: Glycolysis: 2 ATP invested, 4 produced → net 2 ATP. Plus 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.

questions.promptMd: A 50 Ω resistor and a 100 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. The total current from the battery is:
In a saturated fat, the carbon chain contains:

options.label: A
options.text: All single C-C bonds; tightly packed; solid at room temp.

options.label: B
options.text: One or more C=C bonds; kinked chain; liquid at room temp.

questions.explanationMd: Saturation = no double bonds (saturated with H). Tight packing → higher melting point → solid (e.g., butter).

questions.promptMd: Tetrahedral chirality requires:

options.label: A
options.text: Four different substituents on a single sp³ carbon.

questions.explanationMd: A stereocenter requires four DIFFERENT groups attached to a tetrahedral (sp³) carbon — that's the textbook definition of chirality at a center.

questions.promptMd: When ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi under standard physiological conditions, ΔG ≈:
questions.explanationMd: Standard ΔG° is about −30 kJ/mol, but actual cellular conditions (high [ATP]/[ADP][Pi] ratio) make it closer to −50 kJ/mol.

questions.promptMd: Which property of water makes it an effective biological solvent?

options.label: B
options.text: Polar covalent O-H bonds enabling hydrogen bonding.

options.label: C
options.text: High vapor pressure at room temperature.

questions.explanationMd: Polar O-H bonds + bent geometry → strong dipole → solvates ions and polar molecules via hydrogen bonding and dipole interactions.

questions.promptMd: A wave on a string has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 2 m. Its speed is:
Which lipid is the principal building block of cell membranes?
questions.explanationMd: Phospholipids form the bilayer (hydrophilic head + hydrophobic tails). Cholesterol is a regulator (modulates fluidity) but not the bulk material.

questions.promptMd: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a converging lens with focal length 20 cm. The image distance is:
questions.explanationMd: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i → 1/20 = 1/30 + 1/d_i → 1/d_i = 1/60, d_i = 60 cm (real, inverted, magnified).

questions.promptMd:
Passage:

'The notion that cities have a single "character" is, on close inspection, a useful fiction. The Berlin of 1925, with its cabarets and political street violence, has little in common with the Berlin of 1980, walled and divided, or the Berlin of today. To speak of "Berlin" as if it possessed an essence that persists across these transformations is to mistake a historical pattern for a metaphysical fact.'

The author's primary purpose is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Defend the idea of urban essences.

options.label: B
options.text: Argue that city identities are historically contingent.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare three eras of Berlin's history.

questions.explanationMd: The author's central claim is that 'character' across eras is illusion — three Berlins, three different cities. That's a historical-contingency argument.

questions.promptMd: Continuing the previous passage: which choice best captures 'a useful fiction'?

options.label: A
options.text: A claim that is literally false but practically convenient.

questions.explanationMd: The phrase pairs 'useful' (practical convenience) with 'fiction' (not literally true) — that's exactly choice A.

questions.promptMd: Same passage. Which inference is best supported?

options.label: B
options.text: Talking about cities-as-essences may be useful but is metaphysically misleading.

questions.explanationMd: B is the precise position the author stakes: useful as shorthand, misleading taken literally. The other choices over- or under-state the claim.

questions.promptMd:
Passage:

'When economists speak of "rational" behavior, they typically mean behavior consistent with stable preferences and well-formed beliefs. This usage strips the ordinary meaning of the word — "reasonable, sensible, justified" — of its moral content.'

The author would most likely AGREE that:

options.label: A
options.text: Economic 'rationality' is too narrow a concept for ordinary moral life.

options.label: B
options.text: Economists should always defer to ordinary language.

questions.explanationMd: The passage frames economists' usage as having dropped the moral content present in ordinary 'rational' — i.e., the technical concept is too narrow for moral life.

questions.promptMd: Same passage. Which scenario WEAKENS the author's claim?

options.label: A
options.text: An economist who explicitly uses 'rational' in the moral sense.

options.label: B
options.text: A textbook defining rationality as preference consistency.

questions.explanationMd: The claim is that economists strip moral content. An economist preserving moral content would be a counterexample.

questions.promptMd:
Passage:

'The Romantic poets' attraction to ruins was less an aesthetic preference than a metaphysical one: the ruin reminded them, by its existence, that everything human was provisional. The same fragment that delighted the eye accused the visitor of pretending otherwise.'

The author treats the Romantic taste for ruins as:

options.label: B
options.text: An expression of philosophical anxiety about impermanence.

questions.explanationMd: The author reframes the aesthetic attraction as a philosophical confrontation with impermanence — the ruin 'accuses' the viewer.

questions.promptMd: Same passage. The phrase 'accused the visitor of pretending otherwise' suggests:

options.label: A
options.text: The visitor was breaking the law.

options.label: B
options.text: The visitor was implicitly claiming permanence by ignoring decay.

options.label: C
options.text: The visitor was literally guilty of a crime.

options.label: D
options.text: The visitor disagreed with the poet.

questions.explanationMd: The 'accusation' is rhetorical: the ruin's existence forces the visitor to face impermanence, exposing any unspoken assumption of permanence.

questions.promptMd: Same passage. Which extension follows logically?

options.label: B
options.text: A culture that systematically demolishes ruins may be uncomfortable with impermanence.

questions.explanationMd: If ruins force confrontation with impermanence, then a culture that erases them might be avoiding that confrontation. B follows; the others overstate or invert.

questions.promptMd:
Passage:

'In ethics, "thick" concepts — courage, cruelty, generosity — combine descriptive and evaluative content in a single word. "Thin" concepts — good, right, ought — separate the two. The recent move toward thin language in moral philosophy may have purchased clarity at the cost of moral texture.'

The author's tone toward 'the recent move toward thin language' is best described as:
questions.explanationMd: 'Purchased clarity at the cost of moral texture' is a measured, mildly skeptical framing — neither endorsement nor outrage.

questions.promptMd: Same passage. Which of the following BEST illustrates a 'thick' concept?

options.label: B
options.text: Saying 'X is courageous,' which describes a behavior AND praises it.

questions.explanationMd: B fuses description (what someone did) with evaluation (it's praiseworthy) — the thick-concept signature. A and D are thin (pure evaluation); C is purely descriptive.

questions.promptMd: Same passage. Which scenario would COUNT AGAINST the author's worry?

options.label: A
options.text: Translating thick concepts into thin concepts loses no moral content in practice.

options.label: B
options.text: Thin concepts are more confusing than thick ones.

options.label: D
options.text: Moral disagreement persists in any vocabulary.

questions.explanationMd: The author worries that the move loses moral texture. Showing it loses NO moral content is the direct rebuttal.

questions.promptMd:
Passage:

'Public health interventions are often evaluated by lives saved per dollar. This metric is both indispensable and treacherous: indispensable because resources are finite, treacherous because lives at the margin are not interchangeable with lives at the median.'

The author's central claim is that the lives-per-dollar metric:

options.label: B
options.text: Is necessary but flattens morally relevant distinctions.

questions.explanationMd: The 'indispensable and treacherous' framing names both sides: needed in practice, but elides moral nuance ('lives at the margin are not interchangeable with lives at the median').

questions.promptMd: Same passage. The phrase 'lives at the margin are not interchangeable with lives at the median' most likely means:

options.label: A
options.text: All lives have the same statistical value.

options.label: B
options.text: The expected last person saved by a program is morally distinct from a typical beneficiary.

options.label: D
options.text: Statistics doesn't apply to public health.

questions.explanationMd: B captures the technical economists' notion: the marginal beneficiary (the next person served) faces a different choice set than the median, and the author treats them as morally non-fungible.

sections.title: Biological and Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems

questions.promptMd: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative because:

options.label: A
options.text: Each new strand contains a mix of old and new nucleotides.

options.label: B
options.text: Each daughter molecule has one parental and one new strand.

options.label: C
options.text: Both daughter molecules retain only old strands.

options.label: D
options.text: Replication conserves the total amount of DNA.

questions.explanationMd: Meselson-Stahl established each daughter helix carries one parent strand + one new strand — semi-conservative.

questions.promptMd: Which organelle is the primary site of ATP production in eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanationMd: Mitochondria carry out the electron transport chain + oxidative phosphorylation, which generate the bulk of cellular ATP.

questions.promptMd: The structural component shared by ALL amino acids is:

options.label: B
options.text: A central α-carbon bonded to NH₂, COOH, H, and a side chain (R).

questions.explanationMd: Every amino acid shares the α-carbon backbone (amino group, carboxylic acid, hydrogen, R group); only the R group varies.

questions.promptMd: Translation begins when:

options.label: A
options.text: The small ribosomal subunit binds the start codon (AUG).

options.label: B
options.text: The large ribosomal subunit reads the promoter.

questions.explanationMd: Initiation: small subunit + initiator tRNA (Met) bind the start codon AUG, then the large subunit joins.

questions.promptMd: An autosomal recessive disorder requires:

options.label: A
options.text: One copy of the affected allele on an autosome.

options.label: B
options.text: Two copies of the affected allele on an autosome.

options.label: C
options.text: One copy of the affected allele on the X chromosome.

options.label: D
options.text: A new mutation in every generation.

questions.explanationMd: Recessive = needs two affected alleles to manifest. Autosomal = on a non-sex chromosome.

questions.promptMd: Which best describes the function of restriction enzymes?

options.label: B
options.text: They cut DNA at specific recognition sequences.

questions.explanationMd: Restriction endonucleases cleave DNA at specific palindromic recognition sites — the basis of molecular cloning.

questions.promptMd: The Krebs cycle (TCA) per acetyl-CoA produces:
questions.explanationMd: Per turn (per acetyl-CoA): 1 GTP/ATP, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 2 CO₂.

questions.promptMd: A nonsense mutation results in:

options.label: A
options.text: A premature stop codon → truncated protein.

options.label: B
options.text: Substitution of one amino acid for another.

options.label: C
options.text: A silent change with no protein effect.

questions.explanationMd: Nonsense mutations introduce a stop codon prematurely, truncating the protein. (Missense → A; silent → C; frameshift → D.)

questions.promptMd: Insulin is secreted by:
questions.explanationMd: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose. Alpha cells secrete glucagon.

questions.promptMd: Which is NOT a feature of the bacterial flagellum?

options.label: A
options.text: Driven by a proton motive force.

questions.explanationMd: 9+2 microtubules describe the EUKARYOTIC flagellum. Bacterial flagella are flagellin polymers powered by the proton motive force; they rotate.

questions.promptMd: Which type of feedback regulates many homeostatic systems (e.g., body temperature)?
questions.explanationMd: Negative feedback — output opposes the initial change — is the dominant regulatory motif in homeostasis.

questions.promptMd: A polysaccharide consisting of α-1,4 + α-1,6 glycosidic bonds and serving as glucose storage in animals is:
questions.explanationMd: Glycogen is the highly branched α-1,4 + α-1,6 glucose polymer used as animal storage. Starch is plant storage; cellulose is β-1,4 (structural); chitin contains N-acetyl glucosamine.

questions.promptMd: An action potential is propagated along an axon primarily through:

options.label: B
options.text: Voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels opening sequentially.

questions.explanationMd: Depolarization opens voltage-gated Na+ channels (Na+ influx); shortly after, voltage-gated K+ channels open (K+ efflux), repolarizing the membrane. The traveling wave is the action potential.

questions.promptMd: Which step of cellular respiration generates the most ATP?
questions.explanationMd: OxPhos generates ~26-28 of the ~32 ATP per glucose. Substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis + Krebs contributes only ~4.

questions.promptMd: In a Hardy-Weinberg population, the allele frequency p = 0.7. The frequency of heterozygotes is:
Which describes the Na+/K+ ATPase pump?

options.label: A
options.text: Pumps 2 Na+ in, 3 K+ out, using ATP.

options.label: B
options.text: Pumps 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, using ATP.

questions.explanationMd: The pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP. The asymmetry creates the resting membrane potential.

questions.promptMd: An immunoglobulin (antibody) consists of:

options.label: A
options.text: Two heavy chains + two light chains held by disulfide bonds.

questions.explanationMd: The Y-shaped IgG quaternary structure has 2 H + 2 L chains linked by disulfide bridges.

questions.promptMd: Which best describes the role of tRNA?

options.label: A
options.text: Carries the genetic code from DNA to ribosome.

options.label: B
options.text: Brings amino acids to the ribosome and pairs with mRNA codons.

questions.explanationMd: tRNA delivers amino acids; its anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon at the ribosome. (mRNA carries the code; rRNA catalyzes; RNA pol II synthesizes mRNA.)

questions.promptMd: A buffer that resists pH change near physiological pH 7.4 most likely contains:
questions.explanationMd: Effective buffering window is pKa ± 1. Phosphate (~7.2) brackets physiological pH; acetate buffers near 4.7, far from 7.4.

questions.promptMd: Which is NOT a step in the central dogma of molecular biology?
questions.explanationMd: Reverse translation is not part of the central dogma. (Reverse transcription, RNA → DNA, exists in retroviruses but isn't 'reverse translation'.)

questions.promptMd: Which of the following is a feature of meiosis but not mitosis?

options.label: A
options.text: DNA replication occurs once before division.

options.label: C
options.text: Daughter cells genetically identical to parent.

questions.explanationMd: Crossing over (synapsis) is unique to meiosis prophase I. Sister chromatid separation occurs in both. DNA replicates once before each.

sections.title: Psychological, Social, and Biological Foundations of Behavior

questions.promptMd: Classical conditioning was first systematically studied by:
questions.explanationMd: Pavlov's dog experiments (bell + food → bell alone elicits salivation) defined classical conditioning. Skinner: operant. Freud: psychoanalysis. Piaget: cognitive development.

questions.promptMd: The Stanford Prison Experiment is most often cited to illustrate:

options.label: B
options.text: The power of social roles to shape behavior.

questions.explanationMd: Zimbardo's study (whatever its methodological flaws) is typically invoked to illustrate how assigned roles can rapidly shape behavior.

questions.promptMd: The hypothalamus is most directly involved in:
questions.explanationMd: The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis (temperature, hunger, thirst, hormones via the pituitary). Cortex handles decisions; hippocampus consolidates memory; motor cortex + cerebellum handle voluntary motion.

questions.promptMd: The Milgram obedience study primarily illustrates:

options.label: A
options.text: How perceived authority can override personal moral judgment.

questions.explanationMd: Milgram showed ordinary participants would deliver (apparent) painful shocks when instructed by an authority figure, even when distressed.

questions.promptMd: Working memory, in Baddeley's model, includes which subsystems?

options.label: A
options.text: Phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive (and later, episodic buffer).

options.label: B
options.text: Sensory register and long-term store only.

questions.explanationMd: Baddeley's working memory: a central executive controls a phonological loop (verbal) + visuospatial sketchpad; an episodic buffer was added in 2000.

questions.promptMd: Which is a feature of Type 1 (System 1) thinking in Kahneman's dual-process theory?
questions.explanationMd: System 1 is fast + automatic, prone to heuristics + biases. System 2 is slow + deliberate.

questions.promptMd: Erikson's stage of 'identity vs. role confusion' typically occurs in:
questions.explanationMd: Identity formation is the central crisis of adolescence in Erikson's eight-stage model.

questions.promptMd: A neurotransmitter associated with reward, motivation, and movement is:
questions.explanationMd: Dopamine pathways underlie reward (mesolimbic) + motor control (nigrostriatal). GABA is the main inhibitory NT; ACh acts at NMJ + autonomics; glutamate is the main excitatory NT.

questions.promptMd: The 'just-world hypothesis' is a tendency to believe:

options.label: A
options.text: People generally get what they deserve.

questions.explanationMd: Just-world: a cognitive bias that the world rewards good behavior + punishes bad — often used to rationalize victims' suffering.

questions.promptMd: A schedule of reinforcement that produces high, steady response rates and is most resistant to extinction is:
questions.explanationMd: Variable-ratio (e.g., gambling) generates the most persistent responding because reward is unpredictable — the organism keeps trying.

questions.promptMd: Cognitive dissonance is reduced most often by:

options.label: A
options.text: Changing one's behavior, attitudes, or both, until they align.

questions.explanationMd: Festinger's dissonance: when behavior + belief conflict, people adjust one (often the belief, post-hoc) to restore consistency.

questions.promptMd: Maslow's hierarchy places which need at the lowest (most foundational) level?
questions.explanationMd: Maslow's pyramid: physiological (food/water/sleep) → safety → belonging → esteem → self-actualization.

questions.promptMd: The 'mere exposure effect' refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: Increased liking of stimuli through repeated exposure.

questions.explanationMd: Zajonc's mere-exposure: repeated exposure to a neutral stimulus increases preference for it — a robust, replicated effect.

questions.promptMd: Conformity is most strongly increased by:

options.label: A
options.text: Public response in unanimous large groups.

questions.explanationMd: Asch's line studies: conformity rises with public + unanimous + larger groups; one dissenter dramatically reduces it.

questions.promptMd: Which is consistent with the cognitive theory of emotion (Schachter-Singer)?

options.label: A
options.text: Emotion = physiological arousal + cognitive label of the situation.

options.label: C
options.text: Emotion arises before any bodily change.

questions.explanationMd: Schachter-Singer's two-factor theory: arousal is interpreted via situational cues, and the emotion experienced reflects both.

questions.promptMd: Diffusion of responsibility (bystander effect) predicts that:

options.label: A
options.text: Helping behavior decreases as the number of bystanders increases.

options.label: B
options.text: Helping increases monotonically with crowd size.

options.label: D
options.text: Helping is unrelated to group size.

questions.explanationMd: Latané + Darley showed individuals in larger crowds are LESS likely to help any one victim — responsibility is diffused.

questions.promptMd: Which best describes the role of REM sleep?

options.label: A
options.text: Memory consolidation, dreaming, paradoxical EEG (active brain, atonic body).

questions.explanationMd: REM is associated with vivid dreams, EEG resembling waking, but with skeletal muscle atonia. Linked to procedural and emotional memory consolidation. Slow-wave is NREM stage 3.

questions.promptMd: Symbolic interactionism, in sociology, focuses on:

options.label: B
options.text: How meaning emerges from face-to-face interactions.

questions.explanationMd: Symbolic interactionism (Mead, Blumer, Goffman) is a micro-sociological tradition: meaning emerges through symbols + interaction.

questions.promptMd: The 'sick role' concept (Parsons) holds that:

options.label: A
options.text: Illness exempts individuals from normal duties but obligates them to seek treatment.

options.label: C
options.text: Illness is caused by social interaction.

questions.explanationMd: Parsons framed illness as a social role: temporarily exempt from normal obligations IF the patient seeks help and tries to recover.
